Besides this, before the spread of Islam in the 7th century CE Afghanistan was a thriving centre of Buddhist and Hindu culture, and the Bamiyan Buddhas stood as symbols of Mahayana Buddhism's reach from India.
s: Part (a): not supported; the chapter does not say India ruled Afghanistan
Part (b): 'mirrored' means resemblance or influence; further evidence such as a thriving Buddhist and Hindu culture or the Bamiyan Buddhas

questions.q:
A Delhi museum plans a hall on India and Afghanistan with four panels: (i) the Uttarapatha carries Buddhism, Hinduism, art and philosophy; (ii) the creation of Pakistan in 1947 complicates access; (iii) the Bamiyan Buddhas are destroyed in 2001; (iv) India helps with the Afghan Parliament building and the Zaranj-Delaram highway. The curator must choose one banner for the entrance: 'A story of loss' or 'A story of lasting ties'.
(a) Put panels (i), (ii) and (iii) in time order.
(b) Which panels show loss or difficulty, and which show continuity?
(c) How many years passed between the events of (ii) and (iii)?
(d) The curator's rule is that the banner must agree with the chapter's own summary of the relationship. Which banner can she use? Defend it with at least two panels and say what the banner leaves out.
questions.a: (a) (i), then (ii), then (iii). (b) Loss or difficulty: (ii) and (iii). Continuity: (i) and (iv). (c) 2001 - 1947 = 54 years. (d) 'A story of lasting ties', because the chapter says India and Afghanistan have, by and large, maintained close and friendly ties despite geopolitical challenges, and the panels on the Uttarapatha and on the Parliament building and highway show it; the 'loss' banner would contradict that summary. The banner leaves out the difficulties of panels (ii) and (iii), which the hall must still show.
s: Part (a): (i), (ii), (iii)
Part (b): (ii) and (iii) as loss; (i) and (iv) as continuity
Part (c): 54 years
Part (d): 'lasting ties' chosen because it agrees with the chapter's summary, defended with two panels, and the panels it leaves out named

questions.q:
Lalremi's family in Aizawl is thinking of renting a stall across the Tio River in Myanmar for 12 months. In a month when the crossing is open, the stall earns a net Rs 12,000; in a month when it is restricted, the family loses Rs 15,000 in rent and wasted stock. In the last 12 months the crossing was open for 7 months and restricted for 5.
(a) What does the Tio River form between the two countries?
(b) Name the agreement that eased crossing and say how many years it had been in force by 2026.
(c) What does the chapter say has happened to free movement in the past couple of years?
(d) If the last year's pattern repeats, find the family's net result. Find also the fewest open months out of 12 that give no loss. Should the family rent the stall? Argue using both figures and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Part of the international boundary between India (Mizoram) and Myanmar. (b) The Land Border Crossing Agreement of 2018; 2026 - 2018 = 8 years. (c) Some restrictions have been placed on free movement across the land border on account of conflicts. (d) 7 x 12,000 = 84,000 and 5 x 15,000 = 75,000, so the net result is +Rs 9,000. With k open months, 12k - 15(12 - k) >= 0 gives k >= 6.67, so at least 7 open months; with only 6 open months the result is -Rs 18,000. Either decision is acceptable if argued: rent, because the 2018 agreement eased movement and trade and last year just reached the break-even of 7 months; do not rent, because the chapter says restrictions have been added in the past couple of years because of conflicts, so one more restricted month turns a Rs 9,000 gain into a loss.
s: Part (a): part of the international boundary
Part (b): 2018 agreement, 8 years; and part (c) restrictions because of conflicts
Part (d): +Rs 9,000 and break-even at 7 open months (6 open gives -Rs 18,000)
Part (d): a decision argued from the margin and the chapter's mention of recent restrictions

questions.q: Write a question to which the answer is 'Mizoram', using the chapter's lists of Indian states along India's borders, and show how the lists give the answer.
questions.a: For example: 'Which northeastern state lies on India's border with Myanmar and also on its land border with Bangladesh?' The Myanmar list is Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram; the Bangladesh list is West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; the only name in both is Mizoram.
s: A clear question that needs a state on two borders
Gives the two lists from the chapter
Shows Mizoram is the only common name

questions.q: Figure described: a map marking four capital cities by their approximate east-west position: New Delhi at 77 degrees E, Islamabad at 73 degrees E, Kabul at 69 degrees E and Tehran at 51 degrees E, with each country's name beside its capital. (a) Using the east-west positions, which country's capital lies between New Delhi and Kabul? (b) How does that position help explain the chapter's remark that Afghanistan 'once' shared a direct land border with India?
questions.a: (a) Islamabad, so Pakistan lies between India and Afghanistan. (b) With Pakistan in between, the creation of Pakistan in 1947 placed a country across the old direct land link, which complicated access between India and Afghanistan.
s: Part (a): Islamabad, so Pakistan lies between India and Afghanistan
Part (b): the creation of Pakistan in 1947 ended the direct land border and complicated access

questions.q: A headline reads: 'Closed doors: India cut off from Myanmar and Afghanistan.' Evaluate it for each country. For each, give one fact from the chapter that supports 'closed' and one that goes against it, and then give your overall verdict.
questions.a: Myanmar, supporting 'closed': restrictions have been placed on free movement across the land border on account of conflicts. Against: the 2018 agreement eased movement, boosted trade and connectivity, and Myanmar is India's gateway to Southeast Asia. Afghanistan, supporting 'closed': the creation of Pakistan in 1947 complicated direct access. Against: India and Afghanistan have by and large kept close and friendly ties, and India has supported education, healthcare and infrastructure there. Verdict: the headline overstates; access is harder in both, but the ties continue.
s: Myanmar: a fact for the headline (restrictions because of conflicts)
Myanmar: a fact against (2018 agreement, gateway)
Afghanistan: a fact for the headline (1947 complicated access)
Afghanistan: a fact against (friendly ties, support projects)
An overall verdict that the headline overstates

questions.q: A magazine wants to print the 2008 photograph of the Tio River as an 'after' picture to show the effects of the Land Border Crossing Agreement. Give two reasons from the chapter why it cannot serve that purpose.
questions.a: First, the photograph was taken in 2008 and the agreement is dated 2018, ten years later, so it cannot show effects that came afterwards. Second, the chapter presents the picture as showing the river that forms part of the boundary, with Myanmar on one bank and Mizoram on the other, and says nothing about crossing arrangements.
s: Date: 2008 is ten years before the 2018 agreement
Content: the picture shows the river as part of the boundary, not crossing arrangements

questions.q: Sort these six items about India and Afghanistan into 'ancient links' and 'modern links': the Uttarapatha trade route; the kingdoms of Kapisha and Zabul; the Bamiyan Buddhas; the Afghan Parliament building; the Zaranj-Delaram highway; support for education and healthcare. Then explain how the Uttarapatha and the modern highway are linked in the chapter's closing note, and conclude on whether the ties are mainly in the past.
questions.a: Ancient: the Uttarapatha, Kapisha and Zabul (which mirrored Indian systems of governance), and the Bamiyan Buddhas (symbols of Mahayana Buddhism's reach). Modern: the Parliament building, the Zaranj-Delaram highway and support for education and healthcare. Link: the Uttarapatha joined the Ganga plains to Central Asia via Afghanistan, and today's Afghan highway connects to the Asian Highway Network 1 of which parts of NH 44 in India are part; the chapter's closing note says regional connectivity projects aim to revive historical links. Conclusion: the ties are not only in the past; the old Buddhist and Hindu culture was lost in places (the Buddhas were destroyed in 2001) but India's support continues despite ups and downs.
s: Ancient links sorted: Uttarapatha, Kapisha and Zabul, Bamiyan Buddhas
Modern links sorted: Parliament, highway, education and healthcare
Link between Uttarapatha route and the modern highway or connectivity projects
Mentions that the Buddhas were destroyed in 2001
Conclusion that ties continue and are not only in the past

questions.q: Rahul says, 'India's ties with Afghanistan are very old, and the creation of Pakistan in 1947 ended them.' Do you agree? Support your answer.
questions.a: Partly right. The old part is true: the chapter says the connection goes back to ancient times, through the Uttarapatha trade route and the Buddhist and Hindu culture of Afghanistan before the 7th century CE. But the creation of Pakistan in 1947 only complicated access, since Afghanistan once shared a direct land border with India; the chapter says friendly ties have by and large continued, and India has supported education, healthcare and infrastructure there.
s: Verdict: partly right
Supports 'very old' with the Uttarapatha or Buddhist and Hindu culture
Rejects 'ended': access was complicated but ties continued

questions.q: Esha says India's ties with Afghanistan are mainly religious; Faraz says they are mainly about trade routes and development help. Which judgement fits the chapter?
o: Neither alone: the chapter gives religion and ideas along the Uttarapatha in the past, and education, healthcare and infrastructure help today
Esha, because the chapter mentions only Buddhism and Hinduism in the Afghan section
Faraz, because the chapter mentions only roads and the Parliament building
Neither, because the chapter says the ties ended with the creation of Pakistan in 1947
questions.a: The chapter says the Uttarapatha carried Buddhism, Hinduism, art and philosophy, and that India has supported education, healthcare and infrastructure, including the Parliament building and the Zaranj-Delaram highway. So religion and development are both there, and the ties have by and large continued after 1947.

questions.q: A student proposes that SAARC itself should run the shared tsunami-warning network that India set up with Indonesia, Sri Lanka and Thailand. Which point from the chapter shows why this does not fit?
questions.a: SAARC has eight members: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Thailand and Indonesia are not among them; the chapter says other regional groups centred on the Indian Ocean exist for specific purposes. SAARC was formed in 1985.
o: Thailand and Indonesia are not among the eight members of SAARC
SAARC has nine members, including Myanmar and Thailand, so the network could not be shared
SAARC was formed in 2004 after the tsunami and has no members yet
SAARC includes Thailand but leaves out Sri Lanka and Indonesia

questions.q: Two students describe India's ties with Sri Lanka. Anu: 'They are mainly about the civil war, when Tamil families moved to south India.' Bala: 'They go back to the 3rd century BCE; the civil war is one difficult period in a multidimensional partnership.' Which is better supported by the chapter?
o: Bala, because the chapter dates Buddhism's arrival to the 3rd century BCE, calls the partnership multidimensional and says the relationship has not always been smooth
Anu, because the chapter's account of Sri Lanka is mostly about the civil war
Both equally, because the chapter gives the civil war and Buddhism the same weight
Neither, because the chapter says the relationship has always been smooth
questions.a: The chapter says Buddhism was introduced to Sri Lanka in the 3rd century BCE, Hinduism travelled there through its two Epics, and the relationship 'has not always been smooth' because of the civil war from the mid-1980s to around 2010; it calls the partnership multidimensional. So the civil war is one period, not the whole story.

questions.q: A historian wants evidence that the Maldives and India were linked long before the Maldives became independent in 1965. Which item from the chapter serves best?
questions.a: The chapter says Buddhism travelled to the Maldives early on, as established by archaeological finds of ancient Buddhist temples and inscriptions. The water crisis, SAARC (1985) and the Solar Alliance all belong to later periods.
o: Archaeological finds of ancient Buddhist temples and inscriptions
India's quick help during the 2014 water crisis in the capital, Male
Both countries being members of SAARC, which was formed in 1985
The Maldives joining the International Solar Alliance, an Indian initiative

questions.q: The Maldives became independent in 1965, and India was one of the first countries to recognise it. India's quick help after the tsunami came ___ years after that independence.

A student says: 'The Maldives is about 130 km from Minicoy while Sri Lanka is only about 32 km from India at the nearest point, so India's ties with Sri Lanka must be closer.' Evaluate this using culture and crisis help in the chapter.
questions.a: Distance supports the student only in part: 32 km is much less than 130 km. But closeness is more than distance. With Sri Lanka, Buddhism came through Mahendra and Sanghamitra in the 3rd century BCE and Hinduism through the two Epics, and the civil war sent Tamil families to Tamil Nadu. With the Maldives, early Buddhism and influences from Tamil Nadu and Kerala shaped food, dance, language and boat-building, and India helped in the 2004 tsunami, the 2014 water crisis and COVID-19. The chapter calls the Sri Lanka tie multidimensional, and it treats the Maldives as an important neighbour. So distance alone cannot decide which tie is closer.
s: Compares the distances correctly: about 32 km against about 130 km
Gives Sri Lanka culture: Buddhism in the 3rd century BCE, the two Epics, Tamil ties
Gives Maldives culture: early Buddhism and Tamil Nadu and Kerala influences
Gives crisis links: the civil war for Sri Lanka and India's help in 2004, 2014 and COVID-19 for the Maldives
Concludes that distance alone cannot decide closeness

questions.q: A student says: 'Buddhism reached the Maldives before it reached Sri Lanka.' Does the chapter support this? Give what the chapter says about the arrival in each country.
questions.a: No, the chapter does not support it. For Sri Lanka it gives a date and carriers: the 3rd century BCE, through Mahendra and Sanghamitra. For the Maldives it says only that Buddhism travelled there 'early on', as shown by archaeological finds of ancient Buddhist temples and inscriptions, and gives no date, so the two cannot be ranked from the chapter.
s: Verdict: not supported by the chapter
Sri Lanka dated to the 3rd century BCE; Maldives only 'early on' from archaeological finds, with no date

questions.q: Nisha says, 'SAARC includes every country that this chapter calls India's neighbour.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. SAARC has eight members: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. China's Tibet, Myanmar, Iran, Oman, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia are called neighbours in the chapter but are not members.
s: Verdict: disagrees
States the eight members of SAARC
Names at least two neighbours that are not members

questions.q: In 2009 the Maldives' cabinet met at a depth of 4 m below the surface. The chapter says the sea level could rise by 1 metre by the end of the century. If the seabed where the table stood does not change, how deep below the new surface would that table be?
o: 5 m
3 m
4 m
1 m
questions.a: The table stays on the seabed; the sea rises by 1 m, so the water above it is 4 + 1 = 5 m deep. 3 m subtracts the rise, 4 m ignores it, and 1 m gives the rise alone.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives, borrows words from Sanskrit, Prakrit, Tamil, Malayalam and Hindi.
2. SAARC was formed in 1985, twenty years after the Maldives became independent in 1965.
3. India helped the Maldives in the 2014 water crisis in Male, ten years before the 2004 tsunami.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 is correct: the chapter lists Sanskrit, Prakrit, Tamil, Malayalam and Hindi. 2 is correct: 1985 - 1965 = 20 years. 3 reverses the order: the tsunami was in 2004 and the water crisis in 2014, so the crisis came ten years after the tsunami.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Many Tamil families from Sri Lanka moved to south India, especially Tamil Nadu, during the civil war.
Reason (R): The families had to leave Sri Lanka because of the fighting between the Sinhalese majority and the Tamil minority.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are stated in the chapter and R explains A: because of the fighting, many Tamil families had to leave Sri Lanka and move to south India, especially Tamil Nadu. (The Tamil minority's close cultural ties to India are a separate fact; the chapter gives the fighting as the reason they left.)
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A shopkeeper in Male sells fish ('mas') and a boat ('dhoni'), calls the king 'raajje' and a chicken 'kukulhu', and a cinema owner talks of a 'filmu'. Which sorting matches the chapter?
o: Echoes a Sanskrit word: mas and raajje. Shares roots with Tamil and Malayalam: dhoni and kukulhu. Modern Hindi: filmu
Echoes a Sanskrit word: mas and dhoni. Shares roots with Tamil and Malayalam: raajje and kukulhu. Modern Hindi: filmu
Echoes a Sanskrit word: raajje and kukulhu. Shares roots with Tamil and Malayalam: mas and dhoni. Modern Hindi: filmu
Echoes a Sanskrit word: mas, raajje and filmu. Shares roots with Tamil and Malayalam: dhoni and kukulhu. Modern Hindi: none
questions.a: The chapter says raajje (king) and mas (fish) echo the Sanskrit words raja and matsya, dhoni (boat) and kukulhu (chicken) share roots with Tamil and Malayalam, and modern Hindi words like filmu entered everyday use through Bollywood.

questions.q: A student's timeline for a display reads: (i) Buddhism reaches Sri Lanka in the 3rd century CE through Mahendra and Sanghamitra; (ii) SAARC is formed in 1985; (iii) the Maldives becomes independent in 1956; (iv) Sri Lanka's civil war runs from the mid-1980s to around 2010. Two entries are wrong. Find them, correct each, and show that the other two match the chapter.
questions.a: Entry (i) is wrong: Buddhism was introduced in the 3rd century BCE, not CE, by Mahendra and Sanghamitra, the son and daughter of Emperor Ashoka. Entry (iii) is wrong: the Maldives became independent in 1965, not 1956. Entries (ii) and (iv) match the chapter: SAARC was formed in 1985 and the civil war ran from the mid-1980s to around 2010.
s: Identifies entry (i) and corrects it to the 3rd century BCE
Identifies entry (iii) and corrects it to 1965
Shows that entries (ii) and (iv) match the chapter

questions.q: A student in Madurai explains to a younger child, in two sentences, why families from across the Palk Strait came to Tamil Nadu. Write the two sentences using chapter facts, and include the width of the strait at its nearest point.
questions.a: Sri Lanka had a civil war from the mid-1980s to around 2010, mainly between the Sinhalese majority and the Tamil minority, and because of the fighting many Tamil families had to leave. They moved to south India, especially Tamil Nadu, which lies across the Palk Strait, only about 32 km wide at its nearest point, and the Tamil minority has close cultural ties to India.
s: Names the civil war between the Sinhalese majority and the Tamil minority as the reason families left
Gives Tamil Nadu and the Palk Strait, about 32 km at the nearest point, with the cultural tie

questions.q:
In 2009 the president and ministers of an island country held a cabinet meeting under the sea. Suppose the highest point of one of its islands is 1.5 m above sea level. The island council has funds for only one first step: either a sea wall for this island alone, or joining other nations in solar cooperation and calling world attention to global warming.
(a) Which country is this, and by how much could its sea level rise by the end of the century, according to the chapter? How much dry height would the island's highest point have left?
(b) Why did the cabinet meet underwater?
(c) Which Indian-led initiative shares solar technology with this country?
(d) Which first step would you choose? Defend it using your answers to (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) The Maldives; up to 1 metre; 1.5 - 1 = 0.5 m. (b) To draw attention to the danger of rising sea levels owing to global warming. (c) The International Solar Alliance. (d) Either choice is acceptable if defended: the sea wall, because only 0.5 m of dry height would be left at the century's end and the island needs protection whatever the world does; or the cooperation and attention, because the chapter ties the danger to global warming, the Maldives itself used the 2009 meeting to draw attention, and the Solar Alliance is described as a joint effort towards sustainability.
s: Part (a): the Maldives, up to 1 metre, leaving 0.5 m
Part (b): to draw attention to rising sea levels owing to global warming
Part (c): the International Solar Alliance
Part (d): a first step chosen and defended with the 0.5 m margin or the global warming link

questions.q: Use three examples from this part of the chapter to show how a shared challenge can become an opportunity for cooperation. Then name one limit on the cooperation in one of the examples.
questions.a: Examples: (1) Rising sea levels threaten the Maldives, which belongs to the International Solar Alliance, an Indian initiative sharing solar research and technology, and its cabinet met underwater in 2009 to draw attention. (2) The 2004 tsunami, the 2014 water crisis in Male and COVID-19 were crises in which India's quick help strengthened the bond and made her the region's trusted first responder. (3) Neighbours formed SAARC in 1985 to promote mutual interests and share resources in science, education and health. Limit: political tensions among some SAARC members have often disrupted its functioning. So challenges bring partners together, but tensions can limit the result.
s: First example with the challenge and the cooperation: climate and the Solar Alliance
Second example: crises and India's quick help
Third example: SAARC and shared interests
One limit: political tensions often disrupt SAARC
A concluding line linking challenge to opportunity

questions.q: A museum label reads: 'Sri Lanka's traditional wooden masks were copied from south India.' Rewrite the label so that it says no more than the chapter does, and name one cultural link between India and Sri Lanka that the chapter states without hedging.
questions.a: The chapter says the tradition 'may have connections with similar mask-making traditions in India, particularly from south India', so the label should say that the masks may be connected, not that they were copied. A firmly stated link: Buddhism was introduced to Sri Lanka in the 3rd century BCE by Mahendra and Sanghamitra, or Hinduism travelled there through its two Epics.
s: Rewrites the label with 'may have connections' with mask-making traditions in India, particularly south India
Names a firm link: Buddhism through Mahendra and Sanghamitra, or Hinduism through the two Epics

questions.q: Compare how the chapter describes the arrival of Buddhism in Sri Lanka and in China: who or what is said to have carried it in each case, and how exactly is each dated?
questions.a: Sri Lanka: carried by named people, Mahendra and Sanghamitra, the son and daughter of Emperor Ashoka, in the 3rd century BCE. China: it reached China 'around the 1st century CE' via trade and pilgrimage routes, with no named carriers for that first arrival, and the date is given as approximate.
s: Sri Lanka: Mahendra and Sanghamitra, 3rd century BCE
China: trade and pilgrimage routes, around the 1st century CE, with no named carriers

questions.q: Write a question whose answer is '98 km', using two distances from the chapter, and show the working.
questions.a: For example: 'By how much is the Maldives' nearest distance from Minicoy greater than the gap of the Palk Strait at its nearest point?' Working: the Maldives is about 130 km from Minicoy and the Palk Strait is about 32 km at its nearest point, so 130 - 32 = 98 km.
s: Uses the two chapter distances: about 130 km and about 32 km
A clear question that asks for their difference

questions.q: A ship sets out from Minicoy for the Maldives at a steady 26 km per hour (an assumed speed), using the distance the chapter gives. (a) How many hours does the voyage take? (b) At the same speed, how long would a crossing of the Palk Strait at its nearest point take, and by about how many hours is the Minicoy voyage longer? (The two distances are measured differently, so treat the comparison as rough.)
questions.a: (a) The chapter gives about 130 km, so 130 / 26 = 5 hours. (b) The Palk Strait is about 32 km at its nearest point: 32 / 26 = about 1.2 hours. The Minicoy voyage is longer by 5 - 1.2 = about 3.8 hours.
s: Part (a): 5 hours (130 / 26)
Part (b): about 1.2 hours for 32 km, so the Minicoy voyage is about 3.8 hours longer

questions.q:
A Class 7 class in Chennai prepares a display on India's island neighbours with six entries: (1) Mahendra and Sanghamitra bring Buddhism to Sri Lanka; (2) Hinduism reaches Sri Lanka through its two Epics; (3) the Boduberu dance echoes Tamil rhythms in the Maldives; (4) India helps the Maldives after the 2004 tsunami; (5) India helps in the 2014 water crisis in Male; (6) India helps during the COVID-19 pandemic. The class must choose one heading.
(a) Which entries concern Sri Lanka and which the Maldives?
(b) How many years separate the help of entry (4) from the help of entry (5)?
(c) How many of the six entries show India helping in a crisis?
(d) Which heading suits the display better, 'Ancient Bonds' or 'Friends in Need'? Justify with the entries, and say what the other heading would leave out.
questions.a: (a) Entries (1) and (2) concern Sri Lanka; (3) to (6) concern the Maldives. (b) 2014 - 2004 = 10 years. (c) Three: entries (4), (5) and (6). (d) Either heading is acceptable if justified and the cost is named: 'Ancient Bonds' covers entries (1) to (3), so both countries appear, but it leaves out the three crisis entries, all about the Maldives; 'Friends in Need' covers the three crisis entries and the chapter's phrase 'trusted first responder', but then Sri Lanka, whose entries are both ancient, has no entry at all.
s: Part (a): (1),(2) Sri Lanka; (3) to (6) Maldives
Part (b)/(c): 10 years and three crisis entries
Part (d): a heading chosen with entries named
Part (d): names what the other heading leaves out

questions.q: A guide in Bangkok says the Dvaravati culture flourished from the 6th to the 11th centuries CE, and that the Ayutthaya Kingdom was founded in 1351. Which statement matches the chapter?
questions.a: Dvaravati derives from Dvaraka, Krishna's city in the Mahabharata; Ayutthaya was named after Ayodhya, the birthplace of Rama. The 11th century to 1351 (the 14th century) is about three centuries. The other options swap the cities or change the gap.
o: Dvaravati recalls Dwarka of the Mahabharata and ended about three centuries before Ayutthaya, named after Ayodhya of the Ramayana, was founded
Dvaravati recalls Ayodhya of the Ramayana and ended about three centuries before Ayutthaya, named after Dwarka of the Mahabharata, was founded
Dvaravati recalls Dwarka of the Mahabharata and ended about six centuries before Ayutthaya, named after Ayodhya of the Ramayana, was founded
Dvaravati recalls Dwarka of the Mahabharata and ended about one century before Ayutthaya, named after Ayodhya of the Ramayana, was founded

questions.q:
Read the statements about India's maritime neighbours.
1. Indonesia is a single large landmass, like the Malay Peninsula.
2. Singapore was a British colony, then a part of Malaysia, and then became a separate nation.
3. The Indian workers who migrated to Malaysia in the 19th and 20th centuries were mainly from north India.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: Indonesia is an archipelago, several large islands and over 17,000 smaller ones. 2 is correct. 3 is false: the workers came mainly from south India.
o: 2 only
1 only
3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Indian influence in Malaysia ended when Islam became the predominant religion by the 15th century.
Reason (R): A script based on India's Brahmi script was adopted in the region around the 4th century CE.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: R is true. A is false: the chapter says the influences remain visible in Malaysian society through art and literature even though Islam became the predominant religion by the 15th century, and Indian workers arrived later still.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: A visitor to Singapore sees a sign in English, Mandarin, Tamil and Malay, and learns that about 9 per cent of residents are of Indian origin, many living in 'Little India'. Which reading matches the chapter?
o: It fits the chapter's account of close cultural and commercial ties between India and Singapore, with Tamil one of four official languages
It shows that Singapore was ruled from south India before it became a British colony
It shows that Indian-origin residents form the largest group in Singapore
It shows that Buddhism is not practised in Singapore, since Tamil is mainly a Hindu language
questions.a: The chapter says Singapore had close cultural and commercial ties with India, that Tamil is one of its four official languages, that about 9 per cent of residents are of Indian origin and that many live in Little India. It says nothing about rule from south India, gives 9 per cent (not the largest group), and says Buddhism is currently the most widely practised religion there.

questions.q: The chapter says some 15,000 people lost their lives in India in the 2004 tsunami and that more than 200,000 were killed across the whole region. Taking 200,000 as the regional total, the number of deaths outside India was at least ___.

A survey team samples 1,000 people in Malaysia and 500 residents of Singapore, with the same shares of Indian origin as the chapter gives for each country. How many people of Indian origin would it expect to find in all?
questions.a: Both countries have about 9 per cent: 9% of 1,000 = 90 and 9% of 500 = 45, so 135 in all. The other options count only Malaysia, round the share to 10 per cent, or use 12 per cent.

questions.q: Bangkok's airport is officially named 'Suvarnabhumi Airport'. A student says the name honours gold found beneath the airport. Which reply fits the chapter?
o: Suvarnabhumi ('golden land') is the name that came to be used for Java, Sumatra and Malaya, which Indian traders visited from a few centuries BCE in search of gold and other valuable resources
Suvarnabhumi was the name of the Ayutthaya Kingdom founded in 1351
Suvarnabhumi means 'lion city' and was the old name of Singapore
Suvarnabhumi is a Thai word with no link to Indian traders or Indian languages
questions.a: The chapter says Indian traders sailed to Southeast Asia from a few centuries BCE in search of gold and other valuable resources and that Java, Sumatra and Malaya came to be known as Suvarnabhumi ('golden land') or Suvarnadvipa; the airport's name echoes that old Indian name. 'Lion city' belongs to Singapore, and Ayutthaya was named after Ayodhya.

questions.q:
Match each piece of evidence in Column A with the country in Column B where the chapter places it.
Column A: 1. A large sculpture of the churning of the ocean at an airport in the capital  2. A currency note carrying Garuda, the vehicle of Vishnu  3. A signboard in four official languages including Tamil  4. A script based on India's Brahmi script adopted around the 4th century CE
Column B: a. Singapore  b. Indonesia  c. Malaysia  d. Thailand
questions.a: The churning of the ocean sculpture is at Bangkok airport (Thailand); the rupiah with Garuda is Indonesian; the four-language signboard is Singapore's; the Brahmi-based script was adopted in the Malay Peninsula (Malaysia). The distractors swap neighbouring pairs.

questions.q: A student says: 'Indian influence in Southeast Asia is only ancient history.' Evaluate this using evidence from the chapter for the ancient period, for the 19th and 20th centuries, and for the present day.
questions.a: Partly true. Ancient: Indian traders and scholars sailed to Thailand from the 3rd century BCE; a Brahmi-based script in Malaysia around the 4th century CE and the Borobudur Stupa of the 8th and 9th centuries CE show deep early influence. 19th and 20th centuries: a large number of Indian workers, mainly from south India, went to Malaysia to work on rubber plantations. Present day: India is one of Malaysia's largest trading partners, Singapore is one of the largest foreign investors in India, and the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway and the shared tsunami warning network show current cooperation. So the influence began long ago but continues in new forms.
s: An ancient example with its period, such as 3rd century BCE traders or the 4th century CE script
A 19th and 20th century example: plantation workers in Malaysia
A present-day economic link such as trade with Malaysia or Singapore's investment in India
A present-day cooperation such as the Trilateral Highway or the early warning network
A verdict that the influence is ancient in origin but continues today

questions.q:
A geography club in Nagapattinam prepares an assembly on the earthquake of 26 December 2004 under the Indian Ocean near Indonesia and the tsunami that followed.
(a) Which three Indian regions were hit hardest, according to the chapter?
(b) Using the chapter's figures of some 15,000 deaths in India and more than 200,000 across the region, find India's share of the region's deaths, at most.
(c) Where is the centre that now alerts India and her neighbours, and what does the network use?
(d) The assembly has time for one headline: 'India's coasts lost 15,000 lives' or 'A disaster that crossed borders needed a shared warning system'. Choose one and defend it with your figures and the chapter, and say what the other headline would leave unsaid.
questions.a: (a) Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. (b) 15,000 / 2,00,000 = 7.5 per cent at most. (c) The Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre in Hyderabad; a network of sensors, satellites and communication links. (d) Either headline is acceptable if defended. The first speaks to the audience in Nagapattinam, since Tamil Nadu was among the hardest hit, but it leaves unsaid that India's 15,000 were at most 7.5 per cent of more than 2,00,000 deaths across the region. The second uses the chapter's account that the waves struck the coasts of many countries and that India joined Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Thailand and others to set up the network, but it says nothing about the local loss.
s: Part (a): Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andaman and Nicobar Islands
Part (b)/(c): 7.5 per cent at most; the Hyderabad centre with sensors, satellites and communication links
Part (d): a headline chosen with figures or chapter facts
Part (d): names what the other headline leaves unsaid

questions.q: Show that the statement 'The Borobudur Stupa is a Hindu temple' cannot be right, using two facts from the chapter.
questions.a: A stupa is a Buddhist shrine that keeps sacred relics, and Borobudur is a stupa. It harbours over 500 statues of the Buddha and many smaller stupas and is the world's largest Buddhist monument. Its mandala design is shared with Hindu and Jaina traditions, but that does not make it a Hindu temple.
s: A stupa is a Buddhist shrine keeping relics, and Borobudur is a stupa
Over 500 Buddha statues and the largest Buddhist monument
The shared mandala symbol does not change its Buddhist character

questions.q:
The exchange committee of a Hyderabad school can pair with one school abroad, and wants its students to meet people of Indian origin. Singapore offers a host ward of 30,000 residents that includes Little India, where 40 per cent of residents are assumed to be of Indian origin. Malaysia offers a host town of 2,50,000 residents that matches the chapter's national share of people of Indian origin.
(a) What share of Malaysia's population is of Indian origin, according to the chapter?
(b) How many people of Indian origin live in the Malaysian town, and how many in the Singapore ward?
(c) How did the Indian community in Malaysia come to settle there?
(d) Which host should the committee choose? Defend your choice with the figures.
questions.a: (a) 9 per cent. (b) Malaysia: 9% of 2,50,000 = 22,500; Singapore ward: 40% of 30,000 = 12,000. (c) In the 19th and 20th centuries a large number of workers, mainly from south India, migrated to Malaysia to work on the rubber plantations. (d) Either is acceptable if defended: Malaysia, because 22,500 is nearly twice 12,000, so the students would meet more people of Indian origin in all; or Singapore, because 40 per cent against 9 per cent means a student walking the ward is far more likely to meet someone of Indian origin in a short visit.
s: Part (a): 9 per cent
Part (c): workers mainly from south India for the rubber plantations in the 19th and 20th centuries
Part (d): a host chosen and defended with the counts or the shares

questions.q: Rohan says: 'Singapore has always been an independent nation, and its name comes from an ancient kingdom called Singapuram, the lion city.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly (a verdict of 'no' is accepted if both halves are named). The name is right: Singapore derives from 'Singapuram' or 'lion city', the name of an ancient kingdom just off the southern tip of present-day Malaysia. 'Always independent' is wrong: after many fluctuations Singapore became a British colony, then a part of Malaysia, and only eventually a separate nation in 1965.
s: Verdict: partly right (or no, with both halves named)
What is right: the name comes from Singapuram, the ancient kingdom called the lion city
What is wrong: Singapore was a British colony and part of Malaysia before becoming a separate nation in 1965

questions.q: Make a timeline of five entries from this part of the chapter, in correct order from earliest to latest, taking these five: Indian traders and scholars sail to Thailand; the Ayutthaya Kingdom is founded; a script based on Brahmi is adopted in the Malay Peninsula; the Dvaravati culture begins to flourish; the Borobudur Stupa is built. Give the date or period of each and say what each shows about Indian influence.
questions.a: 1. Indian traders and scholars sail to what is now Thailand, from the 3rd century BCE: trade and ideas travelled together. 2. A script based on India's Brahmi script is adopted in the Malay Peninsula, around the 4th century CE: Indian writing shaped local writing. 3. The Dvaravati culture begins to flourish, from the 6th century CE: its name recalls Dvaraka, Krishna's city. 4. The Borobudur Stupa is built in Indonesia, in the 8th and 9th centuries CE: Buddhist art with a mandala design. 5. The Ayutthaya Kingdom is founded in 1351: named after Ayodhya, the birthplace of Rama.
s: Correct order of all five entries
Dates or periods given correctly (3rd c BCE, 4th c CE, 6th c CE, 8th-9th c CE, 1351)
Thailand's traders and scholars, and the Brahmi script, each with what they show
Dvaravati and Borobudur each with what they show
Ayutthaya with what it shows (Ayodhya)

questions.q: Write a question whose answer is '614 years', using two dates from the chapter, and show the working.
questions.a: For example: 'How many years after the Ayutthaya Kingdom was founded did Singapore become a separate nation?' Ayutthaya was founded in 1351 and Singapore became a separate nation in 1965, so 1965 - 1351 = 614 years.
s: Uses the two chapter dates, 1351 and 1965
A clear question that asks for the gap

questions.q: True or False: Indian workers settled in Malaysia in large numbers mainly in the 3rd century BCE, when Indian traders first reached the region. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says a large number of Indian workers, mainly from south India, migrated to Malaysia in the 19th and 20th centuries to work as labour on rubber plantations; the contact of the 3rd century BCE was by Indian traders and scholars in Thailand.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the workers came in the 19th and 20th centuries for rubber plantations

questions.q: Compare Thailand and Indonesia: for each, name one way in which an Indian epic or an idea linked with Vishnu appears in public life, and say whether it appears as a name, an object or a performance.
questions.a: Thailand: the monarchs of the current Chakri dynasty are all named Rama (names); stories from the Indian epics also appear in royal ceremonies, dance forms and literature (performance), and a sculpture of the churning of the ocean stands at Bangkok airport (an object). Indonesia: the rupiah carries Garuda, the vahana of Vishnu (an object), and actors perform scenes from the Ramayana (a performance).
s: Thailand: a named example (Chakri kings named Rama, a name; or the airport sculpture, an object; or royal dance, a performance)
Indonesia: Garuda on the rupiah (object) or Ramayana performance (performance)

questions.q: A brochure says: 'The Hyderabad tsunami centre warns India alone, so every other Indian Ocean country must build its own centre.' (a) Correct the first half using the chapter. (b) Use the events of 26 December 2004 to say why a shared network makes sense.
questions.a: (a) The Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre in Hyderabad helps alert not only India but also neighbouring countries, and India set up the network of sensors, satellites and communication links jointly with Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Thailand and other Indian Ocean countries. (b) The giant waves from the earthquake near Indonesia swept across the ocean and struck the coasts of many countries, so a danger that crosses borders is best met by a warning system that also crosses them.
s: Part (a): the centre alerts neighbouring countries too, and the network was set up jointly with Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Thailand and others
Part (b): the waves struck many countries' coasts, so a shared warning network fits

questions.q: Besides its Hindu and Buddhist monuments, the chapter gives several links between India and Indonesia. Name the link the chapter dates earliest, and one more link of a different kind.
questions.a: The earliest dated link is early maritime trade between Indian kingdoms and the large islands of Java and Sumatra, over 2,000 years ago. One more link, any of: the collaboration between Nalanda and the Muara Jambi temple complex; Islam travelling to Indonesia from the shores of India; Garuda on the rupiah; present cooperation on maritime security, defence and disaster relief.
s: Early maritime trade with Java and Sumatra, over 2,000 years ago, named as the earliest dated link
One more link of a different kind named correctly

questions.q: A newspaper calls the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway 'a brand-new idea in India-Thailand relations'. (a) Use the chapter to say why 'brand-new' is wrong. (b) Name the Indian state where the highway starts and one benefit the chapter gives for it.
questions.a: (a) The chapter calls the highway a modern effort to revive and strengthen age-old connections: Indian traders and scholars were sailing to what is now Thailand from the 3rd century BCE. (b) It starts in Manipur; it improves overland connectivity, enhances regional trade and supports greater cooperation among the countries.
s: Part (a): a modern effort to revive age-old links dating from the 3rd century BCE
Part (b): Manipur, and one benefit (connectivity, regional trade or cooperation)

questions.q: A student asks why India helps to develop a port in Iran in order to reach Afghanistan. Which pair of facts from the chapter answers this?
questions.a: The chapter says India is helping to develop Chabahar Port in Iran, which gives India better access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, and the creation of Pakistan in 1947 complicated direct access to Afghanistan. Iran has no land border with India, Chabahar is in Iran, and Afghanistan was not created in 1947.
o: Chabahar eases access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, and Pakistan's creation in 1947 complicated direct access
Chabahar eases access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, and Iran shares a long land border with India itself, so goods can cross
Iran's ports lie on the old Silk Route, and Afghanistan became a separate country only in the year 1947
Chabahar is a port of Oman on the Arabian Sea, and the old Silk Route came to its end in Central Asia, so a port is needed

questions.q:
Read the statements about India's ancient neighbours Iran and Oman.
1. India's contact with Oman is older than the permission to build the Motishwar Mandir by thousands of years.
2. Merchant communities from southern India settled in Oman over the past few centuries.
3. The Persian language belongs to the same language family as Sanskrit and was used as a court language in India by the Mughals and other rulers.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1: contact goes back over 5,000 years, the temple permission is of the early 20th century. 2 is false: the merchant communities came from north-western parts of India. 3 is stated in the chapter.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India is helping to develop Chabahar Port in Iran.
Reason (R): India and Iran have shared close ties since the Bronze Age.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true, but R is not the explanation the chapter gives. The chapter says India and Iran have shared close ties since the Bronze Age, yet it gives the reason for Chabahar as the better access the port provides to Afghanistan and Central Asia.

questions.q: The chapter says people-to-people contact between India and Oman goes back over 5,000 years, and that the Hindu community was allowed to build a Shiva temple in Muscat in the early 20th century. Taking the present as 2024 and the permission as given around 1900 to 1924, about what share of the 5,000-year contact had already passed when the permission came?
questions.a: The permission came about 100 to 124 years ago, so about 4,876 to 4,900 of the 5,000 years had passed: about 98 per cent. About 2 per cent is the share that came after the permission; 50 and 80 per cent do not match the dates.
o: About 98 per cent
About 2 per cent
About 50 per cent
About 80 per cent

questions.q: A student argues: 'India holds joint exercises with all three of Oman's armed forces, so the India-Oman relationship is purely military.' Which chapter fact most directly counters this?
o: People-to-people contact between the two goes back over 5,000 years, to the time of the Harappan civilisation
Oman is India's closest defence partner in the Gulf
Oman is the first country in the region where India holds joint exercises with all three armed forces
The two countries work together on Indian Ocean maritime security
questions.a: The other three facts are all about defence and security. Only the people-to-people contact going back over 5,000 years (and the Indian community of over 10 per cent of Oman's population) shows ties that are not military.

questions.q: A student says: 'The Avesta has parallels with India's Rigveda, so the Avesta must have been composed in India.' Which reply fits the chapter?
o: The chapter says only that the two texts have parallels, which points to linked cultures, and it names the Avesta as the sacred text of Zoroastrianism
The student is right, since the chapter calls the Avesta an Indian text
The student is wrong, since the chapter says the Avesta has no link with the Rigveda
The student is right, since the Mahabharata mentions the Avesta by name
questions.a: The chapter calls the Avesta the ancient sacred text of Zoroastrianism and says it has parallels with India's Rigveda. Parallels show a connection between the two traditions; they do not say where the Avesta was composed. The chapter does not call the Avesta Indian, and it is the Mahabharata that mentions Persians as Parasika.

questions.q: A newspaper says: 'Indians in Oman built their Shiva temple as soon as they arrived.' Which reading fits the chapter?
o: Merchant communities from north-western India settled over the past few centuries, and the Hindu community was allowed to build the temple only in the early 20th century, so the temple came after a long presence
Indians reached Oman only in the early 20th century, and the temple was built straight away
The temple was built in the 3rd millennium BCE by Harappan traders
The Indian community in Oman is entirely made up of recent migrants who built the temple on arrival
questions.a: The chapter says merchant communities from north-western parts of India settled in Oman over the past few centuries, that there is also an indigenous Indian population, and that the Hindu community was allowed to build a Shiva temple in the early 20th century. So the temple followed a long presence rather than the first arrival.

questions.q: The chapter says the Persian language belongs to the same language family as Sanskrit, and that it was used as a court language in India by the Mughals and other rulers. (a) Why might some Persian and Sanskrit words sound alike? (b) Why does the court use of Persian show that the contact was not only between traders?
questions.a: (a) Languages in one family are related and share a common origin, so some words can be alike. (b) A court language is used by rulers and their officials in governing, so the contact reached the level of government and not only the exchange of goods by traders.
s: Part (a): same family means a related, shared origin

questions.q: True or False: The copper ingot from Oman is dated to the 3rd millennium BCE and the Motishwar Mandir was permitted in the early 20th century, so the ingot is more than 3,500 years older than the permission. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The 3rd millennium BCE ends in 2001 BCE, and the early 20th century begins in 1901 CE, so even the latest possible ingot date and the earliest possible permission are about 2,001 + 1,901 - 1 = 3,901 years apart (there is no year 0), which exceeds 3,500.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: even the closest dates, 2001 BCE and 1901 CE, are about 3,900 years apart, more than 3,500

questions.q: Riya says, 'India's contact with Oman is recent, because the Motishwar Mandir was allowed only in the early 20th century.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. The temple shows the permission given in the early 20th century, but the chapter traces contact between India and Oman back over 5,000 years to the Harappan civilisation, and copper ingots dated to the 3rd millennium BCE support it.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Contact over 5,000 years, from the Harappan civilisation
Copper ingot evidence or the temple correctly placed as a later event

questions.q:
A Surat school sets up a museum corner on India and Oman with three exhibits: (i) a copper ingot from Oman dated to the 3rd millennium BCE; (ii) a photograph of the Motishwar Mandir in Muscat, where permission to build was given in the early 20th century; (iii) a photograph of an India-Oman joint military exercise of 2024. The display cabinet holds only two exhibits, and the principal's rule is that the two must span the oldest link and the latest link.
(a) Put the three exhibits in order of age.
(b) The chapter says contact between the two countries goes back over 5,000 years. Taking the present as 2024, show that this fits with an ingot dated to the 3rd millennium BCE.
(c) Which exhibit shows the Indian community living in Oman?
(d) Which two exhibits go in the cabinet under the principal's rule, and what does the display then leave out?
questions.a: (a) Ingot (i), temple (ii), exercise (iii). (b) 2024 - 5,000 = about 2,976 BCE, which lies in the 3rd millennium BCE (3000 to 2001 BCE), so the two statements fit. (c) The Motishwar Mandir photograph (ii). (d) Exhibits (i) and (iii): the oldest link (the 3rd-millennium BCE copper, evidence of contact over 5,000 years) and the latest (the 2024 exercise, showing today's defence cooperation). The display leaves out exhibit (ii), the only one about the Indian community living in Oman.
s: Part (a): ingot, temple, exercise
Part (b): 2024 - 5,000 is about 2,976 BCE, inside the 3rd millennium BCE
Part (c): the Motishwar Mandir photograph
Part (d): exhibits (i) and (iii) under the rule, with the community exhibit (ii) named as what is left out

questions.q: The chapter shows joint stamps issued to mark the strategic partnership between India and Iran for the development of ports. Write three points to show how port development links the past and present of India-Iran relations.
questions.a: Past: sea routes were used in ancient times since Iran's ports were within easy reach of India's west coast. Present: India is helping to develop Chabahar Port, which gives India better access to Afghanistan and Central Asia. Link: in modern times the two countries cooperate in trade, energy and transport, so the joint stamps celebrate a strategic partnership that continues an old maritime connection.
s: Past: sea routes, with Iran's ports within easy reach of India's west coast
Present: Chabahar Port and the access it gives to Afghanistan and Central Asia
Link: modern cooperation in trade, energy and transport continuing the old connection

questions.q: A student says: 'India's ties with Iran are only cultural, while her ties with Oman are only strategic.' Evaluate this using the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is half-true at best. Iran: cultural ties are old, with the Avesta's parallels with the Rigveda, Persian as a court language and the Parsis, but modern ties are practical as well, with cooperation in trade, energy and transport and the development of Chabahar Port. Oman: strategic ties are real, since it is India's closest defence partner in the Gulf with joint exercises of all three armed forces and cooperation on maritime security, but its cultural and community links are very old, with contact over 5,000 years, copper from the Harappan period, over 10 per cent of the population of Indian origin and the Motishwar Mandir. So both countries combine cultural and strategic links.
s: Iran cultural evidence: Avesta, Persian or Parsis
Iran practical evidence: trade, energy, transport or Chabahar
Oman strategic evidence: closest defence partner and joint exercises
Oman cultural evidence: 5,000-year contact, Indian community or the temple
A verdict that both have cultural and strategic sides

questions.q:
A Mumbai firm must deliver 600 tonnes of medical supplies to Kabul. Route A is the old direct land way through the country that lies between India and Afghanistan; it costs Rs 4,600 per tonne when open. Route B is by sea from India's west coast to a port in Iran that India is helping to develop, then by road; it costs Rs 3,400 per tonne by sea and Rs 1,500 per tonne by road.
(a) Which Iranian port would Route B use?
(b) What event of 1947 complicated direct land access between India and Afghanistan?
(c) Find the total cost of each route and the difference.
(d) Which route should the firm choose? Argue using your figures and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Chabahar Port. (b) The creation of Pakistan in 1947. (c) Route A: 600 x 4,600 = Rs 27.6 lakh. Route B: 600 x (3,400 + 1,500) = 600 x 4,900 = Rs 29.4 lakh. Route A is cheaper by Rs 1.8 lakh. (d) Either is acceptable if argued: Route A, because it is cheaper by Rs 1.8 lakh when it is open; or Route B, because the chapter says Chabahar gives India better access to Afghanistan, while direct access has been complicated since 1947, so the extra Rs 1.8 lakh buys a route that the chapter backs.
s: Part (a): Chabahar Port
Part (b): the creation of Pakistan in 1947
Part (c): Rs 27.6 lakh and Rs 29.4 lakh, difference Rs 1.8 lakh
Part (d): a route chosen and argued with the cost difference and the chapter's point about access

questions.q: Using the Avesta, the Mahabharata, the Mughal courts and the Parsis, show that India's contact with Persian culture has been going on in four different periods and ways. Then say what the four together suggest.
questions.a: Ancient texts: the Avesta, the sacred text of Zoroastrianism, has parallels with India's Rigveda. Epic period: the Mahabharata mentions Persians under the name Parasika. Medieval courts: Persian, which belongs to the same language family as Sanskrit, was used as a court language in India by the Mughals and other rulers. Living community: the Parsis of India are a living link with ancient Persian culture. Together they show that the contact is not a single event but has gone on in different forms over a very long time.
s: The Avesta and Rigveda parallels as ancient textual evidence
The Mahabharata mention of Persians as Parasika
Persian as the Mughal court language, from the same family as Sanskrit
The Parsis as a living link
A conclusion that the contact is long and continuous

questions.a: (a) Oman is rich in copper, and a copper ingot from Oman is dated to the 3rd millennium BCE, the time of the Harappan civilisation. (b) The chapter gives the ingot and the location of the copper as clues, but no record of the trade itself, so the trade is an inference, not a proved fact.

Part (b): the trade is inferred from clues, with no direct record given

questions.q: The chapter explains that an ingot is a lump or block of metal put into a shape convenient for transport and reworking. (a) A trader brings 360 kg of copper (an assumed quantity) as ingots of 12 kg each. How many ingots is that? (b) Using the chapter's meaning of 'ingot', say why coppersmiths would prefer their copper to arrive as ingots.
questions.a: (a) 360 / 12 = 30 ingots. (b) An ingot has a shape convenient for transport, so a trader can carry it over a long way, and the metal can be reworked by the coppersmiths into the goods they make.
s: Part (a): 30 ingots (360 / 12)
Part (b): ingots are convenient to carry and can be reworked by coppersmiths
